summary_cards.label: The plain-English version
summary_cards.text: MCP gives AI apps a standard way to reach tools, files, data, and workflows through controlled servers.

summary_cards.label: The builder move
summary_cards.text: Do not start by connecting everything. Start with one repeated workflow and one safe tool.

summary_cards.label: The risk to manage
summary_cards.text: Tool access turns AI from drafting partner into operator. Permissions, review, and logs matter.

sections.heading: The model asks. The client brokers. The server exposes capabilities.
sections.body: MCP is an open protocol for connecting AI hosts to servers that expose capabilities. The point is not magic. The point is a shared contract, so builders do not need custom glue code for every app, tool, and data source.
bullets: Host: the AI app or agent experience where the user works.
Client: the protocol-speaking connector inside that host.
Server: the service that exposes capabilities over MCP.
Capability: a tool, resource, or prompt the assistant can discover and use.

sections.heading: Tools, resources, and prompts are the core pieces.
sections.body: A useful MCP setup is not magic. It is a small menu of capabilities the assistant can call when the workflow needs them.

cards.label: Tool
cards.text: An action with defined inputs and outputs, like search issues, query a database, create a branch, or open a browser page.

cards.label: Resource
cards.text: Readable context, like a file, schema, document, ticket, or knowledge base entry.

cards.label: Prompt
cards.text: A reusable instruction pattern, like summarize this repo, draft a release note, or analyze this issue queue.

bullets: If the model needs to do something, think tool.
If the model needs to read something, think resource.
If the team needs a repeatable instruction pattern, think prompt.

sections.heading: Use MCP when the workflow repeats.
sections.body: If you only need one answer, chat may be enough. If the assistant repeatedly needs the same tool, file, API, or system of record, MCP starts to make sense.
bullets: Good fit: repeated work with clear inputs and outputs.
Good fit: read-only access to context the assistant needs often.
Good fit: team workflows where the same tool connection can be reused.
Bad fit: one-off tasks, unclear data boundaries, or sensitive writes without approval.

sections.heading: Start with one safe integration.
sections.body: The first win is not a giant agent stack. The first win is a narrow capability that removes repeated copy-paste and still gives humans control.
checklist: Name one workflow you repeat every week.
Write the outcome in one sentence.
List the minimum context the assistant needs.
Define the exact jobs the server should support.
Start with the minimum set of tools and resources.
Write tight input schemas and predictable outputs.
Decide transport and authentication before rollout.
Add a human review point before any write action.
Log what the tool did and what it touched.
Test with an inspector or low-risk workflow before broader use.

sections.heading: MCP makes permissions a product decision.
sections.body: Once an assistant can use tools, security stops being an afterthought. The safest MCP workflow is scoped, inspectable, and easy to turn off.
bullets: Use authentication for every sensitive endpoint.
Authorize per tool and per resource, not only per server.
Use least privilege credentials.
Add explicit allowlists for dangerous actions.
Keep secrets out of prompts and generated content.
Prefer read-only until the workflow proves value.
Require approval before writes, deletes, payments, or messages.
Use rate limits, timeouts, and clear failure behavior.
Keep logs so a human can understand what happened.

guide.starter_prompt: I want to design one safe MCP workflow. Ask me for the workflow, the tool or data source, the minimum context needed, the action the assistant should take, the risk level, the approval point, and the log I should keep. Then give me a small first version that starts read-only.
glossary: Model Context Protocol, a standard for connecting AI apps to external capabilities.
The AI app or agent environment where the user works.
The protocol layer that connects the host to MCP servers.
The service that exposes tools, resources, or prompts.
A callable action the assistant can use.
How the client and server communicate, often local stdio or remote HTTP.
The boundary around what the assistant can access or do.

repo_reading_list.why: Reference servers show the core patterns and also warn that examples are not production-ready by default.
The TypeScript SDK is useful for understanding the server and client primitives in a common web stack.
The Python SDK is useful for data, automation, and scripting workflows.

Inspector-style tooling reminds builders to test the server before putting it inside real work.

guide.updated_label: Built for teams designing AI agents
guide.hero_promise: A builder's field guide to designing AI agents as an org chart of roles, mandates, handoffs, and decision rights.

summary_cards.label: The plain-English version
summary_cards.text: An AI org chart turns agents into accountable roles with clear outcomes, not loose bots built around isolated tasks.

summary_cards.label: The builder move
summary_cards.text: Start with the outcome a great teammate would own, then define the mandate, inputs, outputs, authority, and handoffs.

summary_cards.label: The risk to manage
summary_cards.text: Agents create leverage only when decision rights, approvals, access, and escalation paths are explicit.

sections.heading: Design agents like an organization, not a pile of automations.
sections.body: Most AI projects begin with tasks: write emails, summarize meetings, update project plans. Those wins matter, but they can turn into scattered bots with unclear ownership. A stronger system starts with functions, responsibilities, decision rights, and handoffs.
bullets: Do not start with what the agent does. Start with what the agent is accountable for.
An email draft can be a capability. A Chief of Staff agent is a role with a mandate.

sections.heading: Every role-based agent needs a clear operating contract.
sections.body: Before you give an agent tools, define the role it plays in the system. The contract should make ownership, access, outputs, collaboration, approval, and escalation visible.

rows: What outcome is the agent responsible for?
What can it execute, recommend, or decide?
What context, information, and systems does it need?
What does it create, update, or deliver?
What tasks can it perform in service of its role?
Which people or agents does it work with?
When and to whom does it raise risk or uncertainty?

sections.heading: A simple AI org chart starts with operating needs.
sections.body: The point is not to copy every title in a traditional hierarchy. Start with the coordination, delivery, product, technology, quality, and communication needs the business actually has.
sections.code:
Leadership and coordination
├── Chief of Staff Agent
├── Strategic Research Agent
└── Communications Agent

Planning and delivery
├── Program Manager Agent
├── Project Manager Agent
└── Operations Analyst Agent

Product and technology
├── Technical Architect Agent
├── Product Operations Agent
└── Quality and Risk Agent

sections.heading: Start with four roles that create coordination, delivery, and technical coherence.

cards.label: Chief of Staff Agent
cards.text: Turns leadership priorities, conversations, and decisions into coordinated action. It prepares briefs, tracks commitments, drafts updates, recommends next actions, and escalates strategic commitments, personnel decisions, and external promises.

cards.label: Program Manager Agent
cards.text: Keeps cross-functional initiatives aligned to strategic outcomes. It translates strategy into milestones, manages dependencies and risks, recommends sequencing, and escalates scope, budget, priority, or resourcing changes.

cards.label: Project Manager Agent
cards.text: Moves a defined project from plan to completed outcome. It maintains plans, tracks work, keeps documentation current, proposes timelines, and escalates significant delivery risks or cross-team impacts.

cards.label: Technical Architect Agent
cards.text: Protects technical coherence as systems, tools, and integrations evolve. It evaluates options, documents architecture decisions, recommends standards, and escalates material security, cost, compliance, or irreversible platform decisions.

sections.heading: Build your AI org chart from outcomes to handoffs.
checklist: Start with outcomes, not tools. Name repeatable outcomes such as leadership alignment, reliable delivery, customer follow-through, and sound technical decisions.
Name the role that would own that outcome. If you hired a great person to own it, what job would they have?
Give the role a focused mandate. Ensure leadership decisions become owned actions is clearer than help the business.
Separate execution, recommendations, and escalation. Agents should move routine work forward without quietly assuming consequential authority.
Design the handoffs. Define what each role transfers, to whom, in what format, and what response it expects.
Pilot a small team first. Begin with two or three roles around one real initiative, then refine before scaling.

sections.heading: The essential handoff flow turns strategy into governed work.
sections.body: Role-based agents become useful when the transfer of context is explicit. Each handoff should make the next move clearer and keep consequential choices with a human leader.
sections.code:
Chief of Staff
  → turns leadership priorities into an initiative brief
Program Manager
  → turns the brief into milestones, dependencies, and outcomes
Project Manager
  → turns the plan into delivery rhythm and tracked work
Technical Architect
  → validates feasibility, standards, and technical tradeoffs
Human leader
  → approves consequential choices and resolves conflicts

sections.heading: Governance keeps agent leverage inside human accountability.
bullets: Humans retain accountability for strategy, people, budgets, legal commitments, and high-impact external communication.
Approval requirements should be explicit before an agent sends, publishes, changes, or commits anything consequential.
Maintain a trace of important recommendations, decisions, and handoffs.
Give agents only the information and access needed for their mandate.
Measure agents by the outcomes they improve, not by the number of tasks they complete.
Make escalation easy when priorities conflict, context is missing, or risk is unclear.

sections.heading: Avoid the patterns that make agents harder to trust.

cards.label: The task-bot trap
cards.text: Separate email, meeting-notes, spreadsheet, and research agents fragment accountability. Those are capabilities, not roles.

cards.label: The all-purpose assistant
cards.text: One agent that does everything becomes inconsistent and hard to trust.

cards.label: The invisible manager
cards.text: An agent that makes commitments or reprioritizes work without clear approval rules creates avoidable risk.

cards.label: The org-chart theater problem
cards.text: Executive-sounding labels are meaningless without mandate, context, authority boundaries, and handoffs.

guide.starter_prompt: I want to design one role-based AI agent. Ask me for the agent's mandate, primary stakeholders, inputs, outputs, capabilities, decision rights, handoffs, guardrails, escalation path, and success measures. Then give me a first version that starts with recommendations, not autonomous action.
glossary: An AI agent designed around an accountable business role instead of a single task.
The outcome the agent is responsible for improving or coordinating.
The boundary between what an agent may execute, recommend, decide, or escalate.
Rules that limit access, authority, risk, and external action before the agent acts.
The defined route for raising risk, uncertainty, conflicts, or consequential choices to a human.
A structured transfer of context, output, ownership, or next steps between agents or people.
A coordination role that turns leadership priorities and decisions into owned follow-through.
A cross-functional planning role that keeps initiatives aligned to outcomes, dependencies, and risks.
A delivery role that turns plans into tracked work, status rhythm, and completed outcomes.
A technical coherence role that reviews feasibility, standards, integrations, security, reliability, and tradeoffs.
The system of roles, authority, handoffs, governance, and measures that makes agents work together.
